rv.q: Mr. Cranston's Johnson is a tour de force of physical and vocal impersonation that never feels like mere mimicry
What he lacks in Johnson’s physical stature – the real president was 6ft 4in

For all his grudge-bearing, his near-paranoia and his sometimes dubiously ethical politicking, Schenkkan’s warts-aplenty Johnson, brought to sharp-elbowed and ultimately moving life by Cox, comes across as a man of integrity, even nobility — as well as subterranean compassion.
Luckily, the drama is more nuanced than that.
If The Great Society often feels as much like history homework as drama, it thrums along on the engine of Brian Cox‘s unimpeachably magnetic performance as LBJ.
But the whole thing nonetheless lacks bite.
Cox himself doesn't really claim the character of LBJ until the second act, when the president stands alone, exposed in all his frailties.
Less easy to overlook is Schenkkan’s kid-gloves treatment of his hero – a tragic hero, but his hero nonetheless.

Not every success story gets a sequel. The Great Society, Robert Schenkkan's follow-up to his Tony-winning play All the Way, renders President Lyndon B Johnson's second term an overstuffed yet still somewhat tedious office drama.
The Great Society offers the serious-minded but less absorbing spectacle of a tired captain at the wheel.
“The Great Society,” a tragedy, needs more than that but instead gets less.
The drama is comprehensive without being compelling.
The Great Society is a lumbering, spiritless mess.
If you weren't alive in the Johnson years, it is a concise and electric summary of the conflicts that led directly to today's divided America.
As entertaining as it is informative, The Great Society is a fitting tribute to one of America's most underappreciated leaders.
If the play feels overstuffed, it’s still an important history lesson.
3/4 Stars "Lyndon B. Johnson play an action-packed drama"
Great Society is so telegraphically busy you dwell more than you really ought to on the rare bits of stage business that are slow.
Cox brings a quotidian ease to this enormous role and drives this impactful show with urgency.
But it is ultimately less satisfying than All The Way.
The characters, including the president, almost never seem to really be talking to each other, but only to be declaiming, and with each line at least doubling as exposition.
I don't see any Tonys on the horizon this time.
Sadly, that adage proves true for “The Great Society,” Robert Schenkkan’s follow-up to his more dynamic 2014 work, “All the Way,” now at the Theatre under Bill Rauch’s competent direction.
More a parade of unfortunate circumstances than an effectively curated biography, The Great Society is an earnest consideration of how even a smart and aspirational leader can be undone by his times.
The LBJ that emerges in “The Great Society” is less a portrait of the man, and more of a sketch.
Unfortunately, this play fails to find a theatrical way to capture this breathtakingly consequential time in U. S. history.
This is an incredibly important play.
Perhaps that’s one of the many reasons that, as a play, it’s anything but great.

You may emerge from The Great Society after two-and-three-quarters hours feeling like the show too began in the last century, your head spinning from the parade of events and people that have passed by.

cn.t: Brian Cox delivers a powerful performance as LBJ, but this overstuffed sequel to "All the Way" drowns in historical detail, resulting in a long-winded, dramatically inert history lesson that fails to match its predecessor's success.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
